notes:
I've gathered notes on every verse of Psalm 30. The traditional reading is well covered. I found very little where Protestant traditions clearly disagree, and nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching about this psalm, so those parts are thin.

**What's missing:** I didn't reach the Methodist (Wesley), Pentecostal, Lutheran, Orthodox or catholic.com sites. Most points come from the older commentaries on studylight.org and biblehub.com, plus Enduring Word, the NET Bible notes and Augustine on newadvent.org. I only saw Augustine in a search preview, so those notes rest on short excerpts.

---

**Title ("A song for the dedication of the temple/house")**
- **What "house" means is the main question.** Enduring Word says Spurgeon and Clarke thought that it was actually written prophetically for the dedication of the temple – which David prepared for, but Solomon built, but Guzik treats it as David's palace. He notes the psalm says nothing about the house itself; rather the focus is on God. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-30/
- **Gill (Baptist):** He records that the Targum and most Jewish commentators took it as the temple. He himself prefers the cleansing of David's house from the wickedness and incest of his son Absalom once the rebellion was over (2 Sam 20:3). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-30.html
- **Pulpit Commentary:** If David wrote it, the "house" must be the altar on Araunah's threshing floor after the plague (2 Sam 24). It adds that the modern Jews still recite it at their Feast of the Dedication. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-30.html
- **Others who agree with the threshing-floor view:** Jamieson-Fausset-Brown links the sackcloth of 1 Chr 21:16 with v. 11 (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/jfu/psalms-30.html). Clarke follows Calmet on the same view (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/psalms-30.html).
- **Poole:** He weighs each option and finds it odd that the psalm has not be one line in it suitable to that occasion. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/30-1.htm
- **Modern-style view:** The Biblical Illustrator thinks the title was added later and probably indicates its later liturgical use, and not its first destination. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/psalms-30.html

**v. 1**
- **"Lifted me up":** The NET note says the verb is used of drawing water from a well. The psalmist was stuck in the pit leading to Sheol and the Lord hauled him up. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=30
- **Ellicott:** The word seems to mean to dangle, so it can mean lowering or raising. https://biblehub.com/psalms/30-1.htm
- **Spurgeon:** He draws a contrast: I lift God up because God lifted me up. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/30-1.htm
- **Guzik:** At his own dedication, David praised God rather than himself. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-30/
- **Gill:** He reads it spiritually as well, as rescue from the "pit" of unregenerate nature or recovery after a fall into sin. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-30.html

**v. 2**
- **Gill:** "Healed" may mean bodily illness, since the Lord is the body's physician too, or "soul diseases" healed by grace. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/30-2.html
- **Jamieson-Fausset-Brown:** Scripture often describes affliction as disease, so relief is pictured as healing (same page).
- **Guzik:** Many commentators think David had recovered from a life-threatening illness. He cites VanGemeren's comparison with Hezekiah's psalm (Isa 38). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-30/

**v. 3**
- **NET note:** "Pit" can mean the grave or the realm of the dead. The written Hebrew text says "from those descending into the pit," while the marginal reading says "so that I did not go down." https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=30
- **Gill:** He notes the same two readings and says the sense is the same. He takes "soul" to mean his life was near the grave, not that the soul dies. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-30.html
- **Guzik:** We can't tell whether this was a near-death experience or a narrow escape. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-30/

**v. 4**
- **Matthew Henry:** God's holiness brings terror to the wicked and comfort to the godly. Being able to rejoice in it is a sign that we share in it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/Psa/Psa_030.cfm
- **"His holy name":** The Preacher's Homiletical Commentary says it literally means "His holy memorial," echoing Exodus 3:15. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/phc/psalms-30.html
- **Gill:** He extends "holiness" to Christ's holiness credited to believers and the Spirit's work of making them holy. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-30.html

**v. 5**
- **Guzik:** He puts it in New Testament terms: God's discipline lasts a moment, but His grace lasts forever. He quotes Boice that this is not mere "cheer up," but God's favour versus His disfavour. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-30/
- **Pulpit Commentary:** It is literally "a moment in his anger, a lifetime in his favour." God's anger is brief toward those who repent and confess. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/psalms-30.html
- **Barnes:** "Joy" literally means singing or shouting. With God's friendship, sorrow is always temporary. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/30-5.html
- **Gill:** He holds that anger is not truly in God toward His people. It exists only in how they perceive His chastening. He looks finally to the "resurrection morn." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-30.html
- **Possible difference of emphasis:** Gill (a Calvinist Baptist) denies real anger toward believers. The Pulpit Commentary speaks of real but short anger toward those who repent. This is my own comparison; neither source sets itself against the other.

**v. 6**
- **Calvin (Reformed):** David admits he was justly punished for "foolish and rash security." This kind of carnal confidence creeps up on believers in good times. Calvin contrasts it with the believer's "pious security," which rests on God's promise. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/30-6.html
- **Ellicott:** "Prosperity" is better translated "security." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/30-6.htm
- **Pulpit Commentary:** It ties this pride to David's census, which brought the plague. https://studylight.org/commentaries/tpc/psalms-30.html
- **Gill (Baptist, Calvinist):** Believers really can never be moved from their state of justification and grace. They can be moved in how they practise their faith, especially when self-confident. This is the clearest doctrinal note specific to one tradition that I found. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-30.html
- **Coffman (Arminian, Restoration Movement):** He titles this section "David's confession of sin." I saw no further detail. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/30-6.html
- **A sermon on Bible Hub's v. 6 page** compares three people who say "I shall not be moved": the wicked, a good man lulled by easy times, and the believer who trusts that God is at his right hand. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/psalms/30-6.htm

**v. 7**
- **Guzik:** David's strength came from God's favour, not his prosperity. "Hiding your face" does not mean God plays hide-and-seek. It means David depended completely on God's presence. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-30/
- **Gill:** God may hide His face while the believer stays safe. Only the believer's inner sense of things changes, so those feelings should not be relied on. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-30.html

**v. 8**
- **Gill:** Crying after a God who seemed to be leaving showed love and some faith. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/psalms-30.html
- **Guzik:** Verses 8–10 are probably what David actually prayed in the crisis mentioned in v. 2. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-30/

**v. 9**
- **Guzik:** This contrasts with Paul's "to die is gain," and shows the Old Testament's shadowy understanding of the afterlife, later clarified by 2 Tim 1:10. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-30/
- **Calvin:** He rejects an alternative reading. For him "blood" means death: what would God gain from my death? https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/30-9.html
- **Barnes:** David could serve God better alive than dead (same page).
- **Constable:** David based his request on God's glory, not his own wishes (same page).
- **Gill:** No blood profits anyone except Christ's (same page).
- **Bible.org (Utley):** In the Old Testament, death was a conscious, but silent, existence. https://bible.org/book/export/html/21516
- **NET note:** The "Pit" is often used as a name for Sheol. https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=30

**v. 10**
- **Guzik:** Beyond his arguments, David simply relies on mercy. He quotes Spurgeon that "be my helper" is a prayer for every situation. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-30/
- **NET:** It translates the line "deliver me!" https://classic.net.bible.org/bible.php?book=Psa&chapter=30

**v. 11**
- **Guzik:** The happy dedication prompted David to remember every time God turned mourning into dancing. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-30/
- **Constable:** The psalmist describes his restored health in terms of the celebrations at Israel's annual feasts. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/30-12.html
- **Augustine (Catholic, Church Fathers):** He reads the whole psalm as about the joy of the Resurrection, for Christ and the whole Church. In v. 11 the Church says God has torn off the veil of my sins, the sadness of my mortality. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/1801030.htm

**v. 12**
- **Matthew Henry:** "Forever" shows a resolve to keep praising and a hope of eternal praise. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/30-12.html
- **Trapp (quoted by Guzik):** David ends as he began, committing himself to lasting thanks. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/psalm/psalm-30.cfm
- **Guzik:** Palaces crumble, but God is thanked forever. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/psalm-30/
- **"My heart":** NET has "my heart," while Perowne, quoted in the Preacher's Homiletical Commentary, has "my glory." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/psalms/30-3.html
